note: L.28099. Attributive modifier.

quote: Adjectives that do not normally occur except as (heads of) attributive modifiers include:
note: L.28093. Members in [1] include damn, frigging, main, mere, utter, very (the adjective), own, sole.

item_id: CLASS:expressive attributives [15] (dear, poor, wretched; bleeding, bloody, fucking)

note: L.28335–28337. Hyphen break at "attributive-". Here meaning is tied to a form property (attributive-only).

quote: These expletives vary considerably in expressive strength, with damn(ed) at the low end of the scale and regarded as quite mild, fucking at the high end
note: L.28338–28340. Places damn(ed) in this class, so the [15] class row applies to DAMN_PRENOM by membership.

quote: the bloody tax inspector
note: L.28333. Also "You’re a bloody genius!" (L.28338).

quote: the truth conditions for [iiib] are exactly the same as those for [iiia].
note: L.2467–2468. Meaning, with no form tie. Grouped with *but* and *even* (see section 3).

quote: a fucking investigation
note: L.28333. The [15] class row applies.

item_id: CLASS:expletive adjective–adverb pairs [15iii] (bleeding, bloody, damn(ed), fucking)
quote: Those in [iii] are representative of expletives which occur as attributive-only adjectives and systematically exclude the ·ly suffix, giving a bloody disgrace vs bloody disgraceful.
note: L.28841–28843. The heading of [15] is "Pairs where there is little if any difference in meaning" (L.28824). This links the PRENOM and DEGREE uses of damn and bloody as a same-form adjective–adverb pair. ·ly is derivation, not P05.

bloody          damn –v

property: takes a modified phrase as head (submodification)
quote: bloody nearly completely useless

note: L.29654. Starred. –v is defined at L.29640: "The items in [31] marked ‘–v’ do not occur with the same sense as modifiers of verbs." Example "damn rude" at L.29642.

quote: Damn and jolly combine with well to form clause-level modifiers with emphatic meaning: I damn/jolly well hope you’re right.
note: L.29660–29662. It's unclear whether *damn well* is DAMN_DEGREE or a separate use.

quote: ∗They are very entertaining the prime minister and her husband.
note: L.4480. Also "very –v" (p. 584, L.29624) and "Since very cannot modify verbs" (p. 553, L.28073–28074). The same property as DAMN_DEGREE, held by a control.

quote: very, very good
note: L.29689. Also "The examples in [ii] illustrate the adverbs that iterate most readily" (L.29690). Nothing on iterating damn or bloody.

quote: The meaning of very in very kind is clearly different from that of the adjective in this very room or the very edge of the cliff
note: L.28820–28821. Very in the p. 553 attributive-only list is this adjective.

item_id: CLASS:degree attributives ending in ·ing [8ii] (blithering, crashing, thumping)

note: L.28204–28205. Expletives aren't listed here; the hedge is "tend to".

note: L.28329–28330 (particularising attributives). "Normally" isn't "never", so this is a questionable N under the brief.

note: L.28302 (modal attributives [13i]).

note: L.28319–28320. Says "mostly" and is silent on probable itself. Modal attributives are listed under types of attributive-only adjective, but nothing denies predicative *probable*, so predicative use is U.

quote: The majority of gradable adverbs have bases formed with ·ly, and the inflectional endings are never attached to bases of this kind
note: L.78940–78941. Grading is analytic: "Most gradable adverbs take analytic forms: softly ∼ more softly ∼ most softly." (L.78937). Quick ∼ quickly is at L.78953–78955.

quote: a category of words that do not combine with other words in integrated syntactic constructions, and have expressive rather than propositional meaning.
note: L.68018–68020. Definitional. The stated exception is the n. 70 NP-complement case (DAMN_NP).

quote: Central members of the interjection category in English are such words as ah, hey, oh, oops, ouch, sh, ugh, wow (or the now dated alas)
note: L.68020–68021. The p. 22 list adds damn, gosh, ooh, whoa (L.1707).

quote: used as expressive exclamations, on their own, or as supplements with clausal anchors
note: L.68022–68023. Covers AH, HEY, OH, OOPS, OUCH, SH, UGH, WOW, ALAS.

quote: Ah, so you were there after all!
note: L.68011. Printed p. 1360 (before the PDF 1381 marker).

note: L.86412. Alas sits inside the clause, not at its edge.

quote: Hey, did you hear the weird report on the evening news?
note: L.69284. Also "Hey, birdbrain!" with a vocative (p. 1652, L.82267).

quote: Damn, we’ve missed the bus again!
a number of words such as blast, bugger, damn, fuck which are primarily verbs, but which in supplements like that in [ii] have lost their verbal meaning
note: L.68023–68025. P01 is Y through class membership (reanalysed as an interjection).

quote: The bastard! Max has taken my chair again
note: L.70551. Given as "cf.", punctuated as a separate exclamation. Parent decides whether this counts as standalone.

note: L.70553–70555. Nothing is stated for the clause-final or medial positions.

quote: the bastard
note: Determiner *the*.

note: L.19481. The definition is at p. 380, L.19474–19475: "the head noun idiot is what is known as an epithet, an emotive expression which serves to indicate annoyance with the individual concerned". The quotation stops at the page edge.

note: L.18112. The same sentence continues with "nor in the exclamatory construction You bastard!"

note: L.26684. Position: "in front, central, or end position" (L.26686). Applies to the vocative use only.

These modifiers are constrained to occur immediately after an interrogative word in head, not dependent, function: ∗[What on earth reason] could they have for rejecting it?
note: L.45907–45909. Examples: "[What the hell] is she trying to do?" (L.45899).

quote: contrast ∗And after that you went [where the hell]?

with which, for this involves selection from an identifiable set
note: L.45904. The preceding words are "hardly compatible" (L.45903), a hedge.

quote: They do not contribute to the propositional meaning, and we will refer to them as emotive modifiers.
note: L.45904–45905. Open-ended membership: "Variants of hell in [iia] are heck, blazes, deuce, dickens, fuck, etc." (L.45905–45906).

quote: They are admissible in corresponding subordinates only in contexts of question-orientation.
note: L.49060–49061. Starred: "∗I recall how on earth you saved her." (L.49056).

note: L.49433. Exhaustive conditional is Y: "whatever the hell that means" (L.49431).

note: L.76888–76889. "but not ∗Why ever?" (L.76890). This would exclude "What the hell?" as a reduced interrogative; I didn't check that against attestation.

quote: What the hell’s she doing?
note: L.80517. Class statement at L.80538–80539: "a monosyllabic interrogative word, alone or followed by one of the emotive modifiers the hell, on earth, ever, etc."

note: L.45914–45915. Contrasts with the emotive modifiers' post-head-only position.

note: L.54338–54339 (wraps). Directly contrasted with "∗And so you want what on earth?"

the yes and no can be regarded as a special type of adjunct, a polarity adjunct, which agrees in polarity with the clause
note: L.42536–42538. CGEL doesn't call them interjections.

note: L.42539–42540. Also "?Yes I will." (L.42561), a ?-marked use of yes to refuse a negative directive.

note: L.3880. The sentence crosses to p. 67.

note: L.68002–68003. Meaning tied to supplement function. Scope is uncertain because it is stated under (h) PPs and AdvPs.
